overview: This record begins while Namibia was still under South African rule. Independence came on 21 March 1990 after a long liberation struggle and international negotiations. Modern Namibia includes many languages and communities, with distinctive achievements in water engineering and living traditions of music, craft and shared celebration.

periods.title: South African rule and liberation
periods.summary: The United Nations ended South Africa’s mandate in 1966, but actual South African rule continued until the independence process.

periods.title: Independent republic
periods.summary: Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990 under a new constitution.

items.text: Hosea Kutako’s appeals against South African rule reached the United Nations through Reverend Michael Scott from 1946. Decades of petitions, political organizing and international debate followed. Independence required Namibians’ sustained efforts, not merely a new name printed on a map.

In 1959, resistance to forced removal from Windhoek’s Old Location ended in deadly violence. Apartheid planners moved Black residents toward Katutura. Museum documentation records doors marked with letters assigning different African groups to separate areas, making racial classification visible in the built environment.

Preparing the 1989 election meant reaching rural voters as well as towns. UNTAG reports that mobile teams covered some 2,200 rural registration points. Elections and the constituent assembly then helped turn a negotiated settlement into institutions for an independent country.

sections.title: Water for a city and a school

items.text: Windhoek began adding highly treated reclaimed wastewater to its drinking-water supply in 1968. In a dry region, engineers found a way to use water again. The achievement depends on treatment and checking water quality; simply reusing dirty water would be a completely different matter.

The newer Goreangab reclamation plant, operating from 2002, uses multiple treatment barriers before its water is blended with other supplies. This is an important sanitation story: wastewater becomes a resource through carefully managed engineering, not through wishing very hard at a tap.

At Onakatumbe Combined School in 2017, handwashing stations stood near classrooms and toilets. Children practiced washing before snacks and after toilet visits. Learning to use soap became part of the school day alongside reading and mathematics.

A broken borehole at King Kauluma Combined School in late 2017 disrupted meals and closed flush toilets. UNICEF’s 2018 account describes pupils bringing small bottles from home until a tanker supplied the school. Water infrastructure mattered to eating, learning and using the loo at once.

For northern Namibia’s Oshituthi shomagongo festival, men carve wooden cups and tools from cattle horns while women prepare baskets and clay pots. Fruit gathering and juice processing involve younger people too. A celebration begins long before anyone arrives to sing or dance.

As women prepare the fermented marula drink, they also share songs, poems, family concerns and craft knowledge. Young people learn by watching and joining the work. The gathering links food preparation to conversation and education, rather than separating those parts of life.

Nama and Damara ancestral music accompanies occasions such as weddings and celebrations welcoming rain. A UNESCO-supported documentation project in 2018 and 2019 worked with community knowledge. Musical skill survives through people teaching and performing it, as well as through recordings.

A written Oshindonga example appears in a 2013 community consent letter: “Omukanda gwepitikilo”, translated there as “Certificate of Consent”. The document authorized a heritage nomination on behalf of northern traditional authorities. Communities were writing their own decision into the preservation process.

The republic’s constitution supplies an English sample: “This Constitution shall be the Supreme Law of Namibia.” In plain language, the constitution is the highest legal authority. The sentence comes from Article 1, linking the written founding document to the new state established in 1990.

ending.text: Namibia continues as an independent republic. The 1945 start of this map record belongs to the period of South African rule; it is not Namibia’s independence date. The decisive constitutional transformation occurred in 1990, while families and cultural communities span both periods.
